cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.q: Does drinking at a young age lead to alcohol problems later on?
cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.
cl_alc_early_drinking_later_problems.but: Only a few small studies followed young people over time; the big survey relied on memory.
how: In a big US survey in 1992, about 4 to 5 in 10 adults who started drinking at 14 or younger had been dependent on alcohol at some time, against 8 in 100 who started at 25 or older. They had to remember their first drink.
A review found only four groups of young people whose first drink was recorded as teenagers and who were followed into adulthood.
Drinking early went with more drinking problems in some of them. In others the link went away once other risks, such as behaviour problems, were taken into account.

In US twins, the twin who drank without permission by about 15 drank more as an adult than the other twin, even in identical twins. But in identical twins it was not clearly linked to signs of an alcohol disorder.

cl_gen_telescoping.q: Do women go from first use to problems faster than men?
cl_gen_telescoping.short: Not shown for women in general. It was seen mostly in people in treatment.
cl_gen_telescoping.but: Every study relied on people remembering ages from years before.
how: The idea came mostly from people in treatment or in Alcoholics Anonymous, who had to remember years later when each step happened.

In a US treatment study, women started getting drunk regularly about 4 years later than men but reached their worst drinking at the same age, about 35. So the steps in between looked shorter, but the differences were small.
In big US surveys of the general population, fewer women than men became dependent on alcohol. Those who did got there about as fast as men, about 6 years after their first drink.
Among people with a cannabis problem in a US survey, women got there about 5 months sooner after first use than men. A review said 2.5 years, which is wrong.

cl_gen_early_drug_use.q: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later?
cl_gen_early_drug_use.short: People who started younger had more lifetime drug problems in these studies.
cl_gen_early_drug_use.but: Adults recalled their first use. Some studies did not date when problems began.
how: In a 1992 US survey of adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs, against about 1 in 7 who started at 21 or older.

In Australian twins, about 48 in 100 who started cannabis before 17 met the study’s drug-problem rules at some time, against 33 in 100 of their co-twins. Its drug-dependence measure was not a full diagnosis.
Comparing twins accounts for growing up in the same home. It cannot rule out other differences, such as friends; results for identical twins alone were not shown.
International surveys also linked a younger start with dependence. Drug-dependence models used only the countries that collected those data.

freq.what: adults who started using drugs at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs at some time
freq.note: US adults in 1992 who had used drugs at least 12 times; ages remembered at one interview.
